abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a groundbreaking topological data analysis framework that fundamentally reframes how we conceptualize image representation in image processing. Conventional methods typically operate within Euclidean spaces, yet the intrinsic structure of natural images often exhibits rich topological properties that remain largely unexplored. We introduce persistent homology operators that extract stable topological features from image manifolds, establishing rigorous theoretical connections between algebraic topology and computational image analysis. The proposed framework treats image ensembles as high-dimensional topological spaces, where critical structural information is encoded in persistent topological features across multiple scales. We develop topological convolution operations that preserve essential geometric and topological characteristics during feature extraction, enabling novel approaches to image segmentation and pattern recognition tasks. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the learned representations exhibit superior robustness to noise and geometric deformations compared to conventional convolutional features. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets for image segmentation, image quality assessment, and pattern recognition validate the paradigm-shifting potential of this approach. The framework achieves substantial improvements in both accuracy and generalization capability, particularly for complex scenes where traditional methods struggle. This work opens new research directions at the intersection of algebraic topology and computer vision, offering a fundamentally different perspective on image representation that transcends the limitations of existing paradigms.

Deep image priors have demonstrated remarkable capability in image restoration tasks without requiring training data, yet the theoretical foundations underlying their effectiveness remain poorly understood. This paper provides a rigorous theoretical analysis that significantly advances our understanding of why randomly initialized convolutional networks can serve as effective priors for inverse problems in image processing. We establish novel convergence guarantees for the optimization dynamics involved in image restoration by leveraging tools from approximation theory and functional analysis. Our analysis reveals fundamental connections between the frequency characteristics of deep priors and their effectiveness across different image restoration tasks including image denoising, image inpainting, and image super-resolution. We prove that the implicit regularization imposed by gradient descent on randomly initialized networks preferentially restores low-frequency components before high-frequency details, explaining the observed behavior in practice. Based on these theoretical insights, we develop an enhanced framework that incorporates explicit frequency-aware regularization, significantly improving both the speed of convergence and the quality of restoration results. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that the theoretically-motivated improvements yield substantial gains over existing deep prior methods. This work bridges the gap between theoretical understanding and practical deployment, providing principled guidance for applying deep priors to various image restoration problems.

Snapshot computational imaging for hyperspectral acquisition has long been constrained by fundamental trade-offs between spectral resolution, spatial resolution, and acquisition speed. This paper introduces an end-to-end computational imaging system that fundamentally restructures the snapshot hyperspectral imaging paradigm through joint optimization of optical encoding and neural reconstruction. We design a novel diffractive optical element with learned spectral coding patterns that capture spectral information across the visible and near-infrared range, replacing traditional dispersive elements that limit system throughput. The reconstruction pipeline employs a physically-informed neural network that incorporates the forward imaging model as a differentiable layer, enabling joint optimization of the optical coding patterns and the reconstruction network weights. This co-design approach eliminates the traditional separation between hardware design and algorithmic processing, creating an integrated computational imaging system where optical and computational components evolve together. The proposed architecture achieves real-time reconstruction at video rates while maintaining high spectral fidelity across 31 spectral bands. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the system achieves unprecedented reconstruction quality compared to existing snapshot methods, particularly in scenarios involving dynamic scenes and low-light conditions. This work establishes a new paradigm for computational imaging that transcends the traditional boundaries between optics and image processing.

Accurate medical image segmentation is critical for computer-aided diagnosis and treatment planning, yet deploying deep learning models in clinical settings remains challenging due to computational constraints and data limitations. This paper presents an efficient medical image segmentation system designed for practical clinical deployment, featuring a lightweight architecture discovered through differentiable neural architecture search tailored specifically for medical imaging applications. Unlike previous approaches that rely on generic architectures, our system incorporates medical imaging-specific inductive biases including organ-specific positional encoding and anatomically-informed attention mechanisms. The architecture search space is carefully designed to balance segmentation accuracy with computational efficiency, producing networks that achieve state-of-the-art performance while requiring minimal computational resources. We develop a novel training strategy that leverages semi-supervised learning to address the scarcity of annotated medical data, significantly reducing the annotation burden while maintaining segmentation quality. The resulting system processes three-dimensional medical volumes including CT scans and MRI with substantially reduced memory footprint and inference time compared to existing methods. Validation across multiple medical imaging modalities demonstrates that our approach achieves competitive accuracy with the best existing segmentation methods while reducing computational costs by an order of magnitude. This work provides a practical solution for deploying accurate medical image analysis in resource-constrained clinical environments.
